E8A01: Fourier analysis breaks a waveform into sine waves. A square wave = a fundamental plus its odd harmonics.
E8A02: Successive approximation is a real ADC type: it homes in on the value bit by bit, like a binary search.
E8A03: Time domain = amplitude vs. time (an oscilloscope). Frequency domain = amplitude vs. frequency (a spectrum analyzer).
E8A04: Dither: add a little noise to the ADC input to smear out quantization noise and steps.
E8A05: A true-RMS meter reads correctly for sine and non-sine waveforms. Average-responding meters are only right for pure sine waves.
E8A06: Unprocessed SSB voice: PEP to average is about 2.5 to 1.
E8A07: The SSB PEP-to-average ratio is set by the characteristics of the speech.
E8A08: Flash ADCs are very fast, which lets an SDR digitize high frequencies directly.
E8A10: A low-pass filter after a DAC smooths the stair-steps, removing sampling artifacts.
E8A11: ADC quality is measured by total harmonic distortion (THD).
E8B02: PM modulation index doesn't depend on the carrier frequency.
E8B05: Deviation ratio = max deviation / max audio frequency = 5 / 3 = 1.67.
E8B07: OFDM is used for amateur digital modes.
E8B08: OFDM: many subcarriers, spaced (orthogonally) so they don't cause intersymbol interference.
E8B09: Deviation ratio = max deviation / highest audio frequency. Like modulation index, but using the extremes.
E8B10: FDM: split the channel into separate frequency bands, each carrying its own data stream.
E8B11: TDM: signals take turns in discrete time slots (as in DMR).
E8C01: QAM: two carriers on the same frequency, 90 deg apart (I and Q), each amplitude-modulated.
E8C02: Symbol rate = how fast the waveform changes state to convey information.
E8C03: Change PSK phase at a zero crossing to avoid sudden jumps, which minimizes bandwidth.
E8C04: PSK31 shapes its data pulses as sinusoids, which minimizes bandwidth.
E8C05: CW bandwidth is about 4 x WPM: 4 x 13 = 52 Hz.
E8C06: An FT8 signal is about 50 Hz wide.
E8C07: FSK bandwidth = baud + 1.2 x shift = 9600 + 1.2 x 4800 = 15,360 Hz = 15.36 kHz.
E8C08: ARQ = automatic repeat request: on an error, ask for the data to be sent again.
E8C09: Gray code: only one bit changes between consecutive values.
E8C10: A more efficient digital code gets a higher data rate in the same bandwidth.
E8C11: Symbol rate and baud are the same thing.
E8C12: CW bandwidth depends on keying speed and shape factor (rise and fall time).
E8C13: A constellation diagram plots each symbol's possible phase and amplitude states.
E8C14: Mesh nodes have IP addresses. It's a network.
E8C15: Mesh nodes find each other with discovery and link establishment protocols.
E8D01: Spread spectrum receivers despread only signals using the same algorithm; everything else is suppressed.
E8D02: Direct sequence: a high-speed bit stream shifts the carrier's phase.
E8D03: Frequency hopping: jump frequencies rapidly following a pseudorandom sequence.
E8D04: Too-fast rise or fall on CW makes key clicks.
E8D05: Fix key clicks by slowing the rise and fall times.
E8D06: Parity bits let some errors be detected (not corrected).
E8D07: AFSK overmodulation comes from too much transmit audio.
E8D08: AFSK distortion from too much audio is measured as IMD.
E8D09: Acceptable IMD on an idling PSK signal: -30 dB or better.
E8D10: Baudot = 5 bits, with 2 shift codes (letters and figures). ASCII = 7 or 8 bits, with no shift codes.
E8D11: ASCII can send both uppercase and lowercase letters.
E9A01: An isotropic radiator is an imaginary, lossless antenna radiating equally in all directions. It's the 0 dBi reference.
E9A03: ERP accounts for all the gains and losses in the system.
E9A04: Feed point impedance changes with antenna height (because of ground interaction).
E9A05: Ground gain: the signal gets stronger from ground reflections near the antenna.
E9A07: Net dB = 7 - 2 - 2.8 - 1.2 = +1 dB. 200 W x 1.26 = 252 W EIRP (gain is in dBi, so the answer is EIRP).
E9A08: The Fresnel zone shrinks as frequency rises, so 5.8 GHz has the smallest.
E9A09: Antenna efficiency = radiation resistance / total resistance.
E9A10: A ground-mounted vertical is only as good as its ground. Lay down radials.
E9A11: A ground-mounted vertical's ground losses depend on soil conductivity.
E9B01: 3 dB beamwidth: the angle between the two points where the main lobe crosses the -3 dB ring. Here that's about 25 deg each side, so 50 deg.
E9B02: Front-to-back: main lobe peak (0 dB) vs. the lobe at 180 deg (about -18 dB), so 18 dB.
E9B03: Front-to-side: main lobe vs. the response at 90 deg (about -14 dB), so 14 dB.
E9B04: E9-2 front-to-back: the peak lobe vs. the response at 180 deg (about -28 dB), so 28 dB.
E9B05: E9-2 is a half circle from 0 to 180 deg, over real ground, showing angles above the horizon: an elevation pattern.
E9B06: The biggest lobe in E9-2 is the lowest one, peaking at about 7.5 deg.
E9B07: Gain doesn't create power. A lossless directional antenna radiates the same total power as an isotropic one; it just concentrates it.
E9B08: Far field: far enough away that the pattern's shape no longer changes with distance.
E9B09: Antenna modeling software (NEC) uses the Method of Moments.
E9B10: Method of Moments: split each wire into segments, each with a uniform current.
E9B11: Fewer than 10 segments per half wave makes the computed feed point impedance unreliable.
E9C01: Half-wave spacing, fed 180 deg out of phase: the signals add along the line of the array. Figure-eight end-fire.
E9C02: Quarter-wave spacing, fed 90 deg out of phase: cardioid (one-directional).
E9C03: Half-wave spacing, fed in phase: the signals add broadside. Figure-eight broadside to the axis.
E9C04: A longer long-wire makes more lobes, with the major lobes moving toward the wire's axis.
E9C05: An OCFD's offset feed point gives a similar impedance on several bands.
E9C06: A terminating resistor makes a long wire or rhombic unidirectional (it absorbs the reverse wave).
E9C07: A folded dipole has about 4 x 72, or roughly 300 ohms, at its feed point.
E9C08: A folded dipole is a half-wave dipole with a second parallel wire joining its ends.
E9C09: G5RV: a center-fed wire with a specific length of open-wire (ladder) line, then a balun and coax.
E9C10: Zepp = an end-fed half-wave dipole (named for the trailing antennas on Zeppelins).
E9C11: Seawater is a near-perfect ground, which boosts a vertical's low-angle radiation.
E9C12: Extended double Zepp: center-fed, 1.25 wavelengths long.
E9C13: Raise a horizontal antenna higher and its lowest lobe drops to a lower takeoff angle (better for DX).
E9C14: Over a downhill slope, the main lobe's takeoff angle decreases in the downhill direction.
E9D01: Double the frequency on the same dish and gain goes up 6 dB (gain scales with the area measured in wavelengths).
E9D02: Circular polarization from two Yagis: cross them at 90 deg on the same boom, driven elements at the same point, fed 90 deg out of phase.
E9D03: The most efficient place for a loading coil on a short whip is near the center.
E9D04: A high X/R loading coil (high Q, low loss) maximizes efficiency.
E9D05: A Yagi's driven element is about 1/2 wavelength.
E9D06: Loading coils raise Q, so SWR bandwidth decreases.
E9D07: Top loading increases current along the radiator, improving radiation efficiency.
E9D08: Higher antenna Q means narrower SWR bandwidth.
E9D09: A short antenna looks capacitive. The loading coil cancels that and brings it to resonance.
E9D10: Below resonance, a whip is electrically short, so its radiation resistance decreases.
E9D11: Two-element Yagi: a reflector gives more gain than a director at normal spacing.
E9D12: Parasitic elements are cut longer (reflector) or shorter (director) than resonance to control their phase.
E9E01: Beta (hairpin) match needs the driven element split and insulated from the boom.
E9E02: Gamma match: shield to the element's center, center conductor tapped part way out on one side.
E9E03: Stub match: a short length of line in parallel with the feed line at or near the feed point.
E9E04: The gamma match's series capacitor cancels the rod's inductive reactance.
E9E05: A hairpin (an inductor) needs a capacitive driven element, cut shorter than 1/2 wave, so the two cancel.
E9E06: Q-section: Z = sqrt(Z1 x Z2) = sqrt(100 x 50), about 71 ohms. 75-ohm line is closest.
E9E07: The reflection coefficient describes how a load interacts with a transmission line.
E9E08: A Wilkinson divider splits power equally into two 50-ohm loads, keeping a 50-ohm input.
E9E09: To shunt-feed a grounded tower, use a gamma match.
E9E11: Phasing lines on multiple driven elements control the radiation pattern.
E9F01: Velocity factor = speed in the line / speed of light.
E9F03: Waves travel slower in coax than in air, so a given physical length is electrically longer.
E9F04: A half-wave line repeats its load: a short at the far end looks like a short (very low impedance).
E9F05: Microstrip: printed traces over a ground plane, giving constant impedance at microwaves.
E9F06: Half wave in meters = 150 / f(MHz) = 150 / 14.1 = 10.6 m (air line, velocity factor about 1).
E9F07: Open-wire (ladder) line has lower loss than plastic-dielectric coax.
E9F08: All of these are true of foam coax: lower voltage rating, lower loss, higher velocity factor.
E9F09: A quarter-wave line inverts its load: shorted at the far end, it looks like an open (very high impedance).
E9F10: Shorter than a quarter wave and shorted = inductive. Memory hook: short-short-L.
E9F11: Shorter than a quarter wave and open = capacitive. (An open line is like capacitor plates.)
E9F12: A quarter wave inverts: open at the far end looks like a short (very low impedance).
E9G01: A Smith chart calculates impedance along transmission lines.
E9G02: Smith chart coordinates: resistance circles and reactance arcs.
E9G03: Smith charts are used to find impedance and SWR along transmission lines.
E9G04: A Smith chart's two families: resistance (circles) and reactance (arcs).
E9G05: A classic Smith chart job: the length and position of a matching stub.
E9G06: The big outer circle, where the reactance arcs end, is the reactance axis.
E9G07: The only straight line on a Smith chart is the resistance axis.
E9G08: Normalize a Smith chart by reassigning the prime center's impedance (for example, 50 ohms = 1.0).
E9G09: Constant-SWR circles, centered on the prime center, are often added.
E9G10: The arcs are constant reactance. The circles are constant resistance.
E9G11: The wavelength scales are in fractions of the line's electrical wavelength.
E9H01: A Beverage should be at least one wavelength long. It's a long, low wire.
E9H02: On 160 and 80 m the noise is huge, so a receiving antenna's directivity matters more than its losses.
E9H03: RDF = peak gain compared to average gain over the hemisphere: how well the antenna favors one direction.
E9H04: An electrostatic shield on a DF loop removes unbalanced capacitive coupling, giving deeper nulls.
E9H05: A small loop has two nulls, 180 deg apart, so it can't tell front from back.
E9H06: Tune a Beverage's termination resistor for the least SWR variation across the band.
E9H07: The Beverage termination resistor absorbs signals arriving from the reverse direction.
E9H08: A sense antenna turns a loop's two nulls into a single null, resolving the 180-degree ambiguity.
E9H09: A terminated single-turn loop (pennant) has a cardioid pattern.
E9H10: More turns and/or more loop area means more output voltage.
E9H11: A cardioid has a single null, which points to the transmitter unambiguously.
